You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test `testPValueNearZero` verifies that the p-value computed by PearsonsCorrelation for nearly perfect correlation in increasing dimensions remains positive and diminishes smoothly near zero. The test constructs a dataset where correlation approaches 1 as the dimension increases, expecting a very small p-value (~1E-303) but not zero.

The reported bug indicates that in `PearsonsCorrelation.getCorrelationPValues`, the precision of the p-value is limited by machine epsilon (approximately 2.2e-16), causing p-values smaller than that threshold to effectively become zero rather than continuing smoothly decreasing. This aligns with the test's comment and symptom that p-values "vanish" at certain large dimensions after a previous fix.

Inspecting the method `PearsonsCorrelation.getCorrelationPValues`, it computes p-values based on the t-distribution cumulative probability on a test statistic derived from correlation coefficient `r`. The calculation uses the formula:

`t = |r * sqrt((nObs - 2) / (1 - r²))|`

and then

`p-value = 2 * (1 - cumulativeProbability(t))`

The precision limit arises because the t-distribution cumulative probability function and floating-point computations cannot produce p-values smaller than the machine epsilon. Once the tail probability computed is smaller than the machine epsilon, the value effectively becomes zero.

Hence, for extremely high correlations (r -> 1), the t-statistic becomes very large, and the survival probability (1 - cumulativeProbability) approaches zero. Due to numerical precision limits, the calculated p-value "jumps" to zero early rather than diminishing continuously.

Overall, the bug occurs because the method does not use an approach that can handle extremely small tail probabilities robustly beyond machine epsilon limits, causing p-values in such cases to be reported as zero instead of a tiny positive number, thus failing the test.

Recent bug reports about numerical solver strictness or ODE integration range handling don't appear relevant to this particular numerical precision issue.

This diagnosis explains why p-values vanish at a certain dimension in the test despite theoretically having nonzero probability, indicating a machine precision limitation in the p-value calculation using TDistribution's cumulativeProbability method.

Next, checking the TDistribution class's implementation or its usage might provide the best location to fix by improving the tail probability calculation to handle very small p-values more robustly. Alternatively, adding a minimal positive floor or using an alternative distribution approximation can help solve this precision issue.
org.apache.commons.math.stat.correlation.PearsonsCorrelation.getCorrelationPValues()

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
